title: Split Array into Consecutive Subsequences
description:
# Split Array into Consecutive Subsequences

You are given an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order.

Determine whether every occurrence in `nums` can be assigned to exactly one subsequence so that all subsequences satisfy both rules:

* Each subsequence is strictly consecutive, meaning every next value is exactly one greater than the previous value.
* Each subsequence has length at least `3`.

A subsequence keeps the relative order of chosen occurrences, but because `nums` is already sorted, each valid subsequence will appear as increasing consecutive values. Return `true` if such a split exists, or `false` otherwise.

## Example 1:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3,3,4,5]
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** One valid split is [1,2,3] and [3,4,5].

## Example 2:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3,3,4,4,5,5]
**Output:** true
**Explanation:** One valid split is [1,2,3,4,5] and [3,4,5].

## Example 3:

**Input:** nums = [1,2,3,4,4,5]
**Output:** false
**Explanation:** The extra 4 cannot be placed into any consecutive subsequence of length at least 3.

## Constraints:

* `1 <= nums.length <= 10^4`
* `-1000 <= nums[i] <= 1000`
* `nums` is sorted in non-decreasing order.

solutions.name: Greedy with Two HashMaps
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain one map for remaining frequencies and another map for how many subsequences are waiting for each next value. When processing a number, first try to append it to a subsequence that already needs it. If none exists, start a new length-three subsequence by reserving `num + 1` and `num + 2`.

## Key Insight

Appending to an existing subsequence is always safer than starting a new one, because a short open subsequence may never reach length three. A new subsequence is allowed only when the next two values are immediately available.

## Complexity Analysis

Each occurrence is processed once and each map operation is expected `O(1)`, so the running time is `O(n)`. The frequency and waiting maps may store `O(n)` distinct values.

solutions.name: Global Min Heap of Active Subsequences
solutions.description:
## Approach

Keep active subsequences in a priority queue ordered by ending value and then by length. Before placing a new number, close and validate every subsequence whose end is too far behind. If the smallest valid end is `num - 1`, extend that shortest compatible subsequence; otherwise start a new one at `num`.

## Key Insight

When several subsequences end at the same value, the shortest one must be extended first. Otherwise a length-one or length-two subsequence can be stranded even though a longer subsequence would already be safe.

## Complexity Analysis

Every occurrence is inserted once and removed once from the heap, giving `O(n log n)` time. The heap can contain `O(n)` active subsequences.

solutions.name: Length Bucket Greedy
solutions.description:
## Approach

Process equal values as a group. Track how many subsequences ending at the previous value have length `1`, length `2`, and length at least `3`. For the current value, all length-one and length-two subsequences must be extended first; leftover occurrences can extend already-valid sequences or start new length-one sequences.

## Key Insight

Only the counts of short and already-valid subsequences matter when moving from one value group to the next. If a gap appears, any length-one or length-two pending sequence immediately makes the split impossible.

## Complexity Analysis

The grouped scan visits each input occurrence once, so the running time is `O(n)`. It stores only three counters and the previous value, so the extra space is `O(1)`.

solutions.name: Tail-Grouped Shortest Length Heaps
solutions.description:
## Approach

Map each ending value to a min-heap of lengths for subsequences ending there. For each number, look at the heap for `num - 1`. If it exists, extend the shortest such subsequence; otherwise start a new length-one subsequence ending at `num`. After all values are placed, every stored length must be at least three.

## Key Insight

Grouping by tail makes the greedy choice explicit: the next value should rescue the shortest compatible subsequence first. This avoids the common mistake of extending a long safe sequence while leaving a length-one sequence unable to finish.

## Complexity Analysis

Each occurrence moves through a heap once, so the worst-case time is `O(n log n)`. The map and heaps store one length per active subsequence, using `O(n)` space.
